Lettre de motivation pour:
Notre mission est de fournir de l’énergie moins chère et plus verte sur le marché Français.

Octopus Energy France, est une entreprise en pleine croissance dans le domaine de l'énergie et reconnue ESS (économie sociale et solidaire).

Nous offrons une meilleure expérience à nos client·es grâce à la transparence, l'honnêteté et la simplicité. Nous voulons faire mieux pour la planète, grâce à un investissement réel long terme dans la production d'énergie renouvelable et un avenir à faible émission de CO2, plus avantageux pour le portefeuille de nos client·es. Nous voulons révolutionner le domaine de l’énergie grâce à nos équipes, notre plateforme et à notre utilisation de données.

Nous nous concentrons sur la satisfaction de nos client·es et il nous tient à coeur de recevoir des avis positifs - nous avons le meilleur score parmi les fournisseurs d'énergie français sur Google Reviews et Trust Pilot.

Kraken technologies

Kraken Technologies est une société du groupe Octopus Energy qui octroie des licences pour la plateforme et le modèle d'exploitation Kraken à des clients du monde entier. Les clients actuels sont à la fois les entreprises de vente au détail d'Octopus Energy dans le monde entier et des clients externes tels que Good Energy, Origin, EDF, E.ON et Queensland Energy - et beaucoup d'autres devraient nous rejoindre au cours des prochaines années !

Notre équipe

Toute la technologie est écrite et entretenue par une équipe d'ingénieurs multidisciplinaire d'environ 450 personnes dans le monde. Il s'agit d'ingénieurs côté serveur, côté client et mobile qui travaillent en étroite collaboration avec des experts UX, des rédacteurs et des concepteurs.

Nous suivons une approche de type Kanban, en utilisant Google docs et Asana pour spécifier et gérer le travail ; Github, CircleCI et Terraform Enterprise dans le cadre d'une infrastructure immuable et d'un pipeline de livraison continue ; et Loggly, Sentry et Cloudwatch pour mesurer les performances et surveiller la production.

Certaines de nos conventions de codage sont open-source.

Octopus est un endroit idéal pour apprendre, travailler avec des ingénieurs talentueux et améliorer tes compétences.

Notre technologie

Côté serveur, nous utilisons principalement Python. La plupart de nos sites web sont propulsés par Django, Django-REST-framework et GraphQL (Graphene).

Nous utilisons fortement AWS, employant la plupart des "Hashistack" (par exemple Packer, Consul, Terraform) dans le cadre d'un pipeline de déploiement continu. Voir, par exemple, Django, ELB health checks et continuous delivery.

Côté client, nous utilisons React, Redux et SASS ; nos applications mobiles sont construites en utilisant du code natif ou React Native.

Ce que tu feras

Nous avons beaucoup de défis de conception difficiles à résoudre. Le marché français de l'énergie est compliqué, obsolète et lourd de processus - il y a énormément de modélisation de domaine que nous devons réussir. Une grande attention aux détails est essentielle.

Nous avons des problèmes techniques difficiles à résoudre. Avec l'arrivée des compteurs intelligents, nous traiterons bientôt des millions de relevés de compteurs par jour. Nous avons besoin de la bonne technologie pour gérer cela en douceur et alimenter en données un pipeline d'apprentissage automatique qui modélise et prédit la consommation.

Tu travailleras pour une entreprise qui lutte contre le changement climatique.

En tant que fournisseur, nous aidons les gens à utiliser des technologies plus vertes et des énergies renouvelables, tout en contribuant à faire évoluer le marché français vers un avenir plus sobre en carbone.

Nous recherchons idéalement une personne ayant des compétences dans les domaines suivants

Python
Django (or equiv. web framework)
Fluent in French, and lever B2 at least in English
Domain modelling
HTTP and REST APIs
Writing robust and fault-tolerant software
Celery and async processing
Postgres
Plus experience in the following would be a bonus:
AWS
Terraform, Packer, Consul
React and Redux


Pourquoi tu vas adorer travailler pour nous

Tu te demandes quel est le salaire pour ce poste ? Demande-le nous ! Lors de notre premier contact, c’est un point que nous abordons toujours, car nous souhaitons réellement faire correspondre ton expérience avec le bon salaire. La raison pour laquelle nous n’en parlons pas ici est que nous avons un certain degré de flexibilité et que nous ne voudrions jamais que le salaire soit une raison pour laquelle quelqu’un.e ne postule pas chez Octopus - ce qui est plus important pour nous est de trouver le bon octofit
Octopus Energy a une culture unique : nous avons gagné le prix de la meilleure entreprise pour laquelle travailler en 2022, sur Glassdoor UK nous avons été élus parmi les 50 meilleurs endroits où travailler en 2022 et notre PDG, Greg, a enregistré un podcast sur notre culture et la façon dont nous donnons du pouvoir à nos employés. En France, nous avons reçus le label Happy at Work, et nous sommes classés dix-huitième sur sur un total de 1 675 structures dans la catégorie des entreprises au sein desquelles les employé·es trouvent le plus de sens.
Nous sommes une organisation où les gens apprennent, décident et construisent plus rapidement. Où ils travaillent de manière autonome, avec des gens extraordinaires, sur des projets qui innovent. Intéressement au capital, flex-office, excellente mutuelle, forfait mobilité douce, prise en charge d’une partie du pass navigo au delà du minimum légal, et même des jours de congés spéciaux pour t’investir dans un projet associatif qui te tient à coeur… nous voulons que ton investissement soit récompensé par des avantages auxquels tu tiens vraiment !


Chez Octopus, nous cherchons des personnes foncièrement bienveillantes et empathiques. L’égalité des chances nous tient à cœur et nous veillons à offrir un environnement de travail inclusif et équitable. Nous t’invitons à postuler, quels que soient ton âge, genre, vie conjugale, couleur, handicap, grossesse ou parentalité, origine, convictions religieuses ou orientation sexuelle.

8. Indictable and Summary Offences
A further classification, which still survives, is that of indictable and summary offences. These terms refer to the mode and venue of trial involved; "indictment" is the process whereby an accused goes to trial before a judge and jury. "Summary" offences, on the other hand, may be dealt with by magistrates. On the whole, indictable offences are more serious.

The maxim actus non facit reum, nisi mens sit rea (the act itself does not constitute guilt unless done with a guilty intent) applies to crimes generally. The prosecution must therefore prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused committed a prohibited act (actus reus) with a guilty intent (mens rea). Some offences do not require a guilty intent, as such, and are accordingly referred to as crimes of strict liability. "The colloquial turn-of-phrase for the domestic Vekllei economy is “functionally moneyless,” but the actual mechanisms of the internal Vekllei market is considerably more complex. While the average Vekllei person is insulated from money and money-management, their Commonwealth is a major entrepôt and has a reputation as an “Atlantic Middleman.” Vekllei’s facilitation of frictionless free trade, large foreign-exchange reserves and received foreign direct investments have resulted in decades of consistent economic growth, and has cemented its reputation as a financial hub between Europe and the Americas.

Vekllei’s history as a trade hub contributes significantly to its perceived neutrality and its reputation as a meeting place for politics and business, and regularly hosts diplomatic missions as a neutral site. It maintains its moneyless primary economy by effectively isolating its primary (domestic) and secondary (international) markets, which are the reason for its twin currencies and its unusual hybrid market system. Because the Vekllei state manages all money as a function of its moneylessness, the international market and foreign trade is strongly characterised by dirigism and fundamentally beholden to the economic management of the Ministry of Commerce, which acts as both a financial regulator and investment bank.

The Vekllei Domestic Market is the turn-of-phrase for the unmoneyed Vekllei economy, including almost all private and public businesses and the majority of trade conducted by ordinary Vekllei people. It is the primary market of Vekllei. For most Vekllei people, the domestic market is the only one with which they will interact in their lives, except for the occasional holiday overseas. The Domestic Market includes all sectors of the Vekllei economy except state trade apparatuses like VKIM.

While the participatory nature of the Domestic Market affects its gross productivity, it is regarded as free, innovative and dynamic. It has a skilled workforce benefitted by a robust education system and a high quality of life. About 40% of Vekllei people were born overseas, and some 15% of the Vekllei workforce remain foreign workers. Foreign workers, unlike domestic ones, are remunerated unless residing under an immigration visa."

Researchers have discovered a link between birth mothers who experienced stressful childhood events and their own children’s behavior problem. The finding held true even though the children were adopted as newborns, raised by their adoptive parents, and were never directly exposed to the stresses their birth mothers had experienced. If a child’s adoptive mother also experienced stressful events as a youth, such as abuse, neglect, violence, or poverty, then the child’s behavior issues were even more pronounced, the researchers found. This study underscores the importance of efforts to prevent child neglect, poverty, and sexual and physical abuse, and to intervene with help and support when children experience them. “We can’t always prevent bad things from happening to young children,” says Leslie Leve, a professor in the University of Oregon College of Education, a scientist with the Prevention Science Institute, and lead author of the study in the journal Development and Psychopathology. “But we can provide behavioral health supports to individuals who have been exposed to childhood trauma or neglect to help them develop coping skills and support networks, so that difficult childhood experiences are less likely to negatively impact them—or the next generation.” In the only study of its kind, Leve and other researchers followed 561 adopted children, their birth parents, and adoptive parents for more than a decade. They recruited participants through 45 adoption agencies in 15 states nationwide. The researchers collected data from the birth parents when children in the study were infants and from the adoptive parents when the children were age 6-7 and again at age 11. The researchers found when birth mothers reported more adverse childhood experiences and other life stress when they were young, their children showed less “effortful control” at age 7. Examples of “effortful control” include the child being able to wait before initiating new activities when asked and being able to easily stop an activity when told “No.” At age 11, the children of these same mothers showed more “externalizing behavior,” such as rule-breaking and aggressive behavior. The study also points the way for additional inquiry. For example, exactly how does stress in one generation become associated with behavior in the next generation? “We know from nonhuman animal studies that stress can change the expression of genes by essentially changing which genes are turned ‘on’ or ‘off’ when passed on to the next generation,” Leve says. “That could be a plausible pathway.” Further, what is the effect of the environment in which the child was raised? “Can we find something positive in the rearing environment, perhaps parents’ warmth or sensitivity, that can help offset the child’s genetic or biologic risk for impulsive or externalizing behavior?” Leve asks. That is the next question the research team is exploring. Additional coauthors are from the University of Oregon; the University of California, Riverside; the University of Cambridge; Penn State; George Washington University; and the University of Pittsburgh. The research was supported by grants from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health & Human Development; the National Institute on Drug Abuse; National Institutes of Health Office of Behavioral and Social Sciences Research; National Institute of Mental Health; National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Disease; National Institute of Health’s Office of the Director; and the Andrew and Virginia Rudd Family Foundation. Source: University of Oregon

The algorithm's performance is modeled by the function \( P(t) \), where \( P(t) = \frac{e^{kt}}{1 + e^{kt}} \) and \( k \) is a constant that depends on specific implementation details. The founder's goal is to maximize the product's efficiency over time.

1. **Optimization Sub-problem:** Given that the product's efficiency over time is represented by \( P(t) \), find the value of \( t \) that maximizes the efficiency. Determine the critical points and ascertain whether they correspond to maximum efficiency. Assume \( k = 0.5 \).

2. **Integration Sub-problem:** To understand the total impact of incorporating the algorithm into the product, the founder also wants to calculate the total efficiency over a specific period. Compute the definite integral of \( P(t) \) from \( t = 0 \) to \( t = T \), where \( T \) is the time horizon for evaluating the product's performance. Assume \( T = 10 \) and \( k = 0.5 \).

A parent organizes a toy swap party with 12 parents participating, each bringing a set of vintage toys. Each parent brings a different number of toys, such that the number of toys each parent brings forms an arithmetic sequence. The parent organizing the event ensures that the total number of toys brought by all the parents is 156.

1. Determine the number of toys brought by the parent who brought the median number of toys.

2. After the swap, each parent leaves with a different number of toys, forming a geometric sequence. If the parent who originally brought the most toys leaves with the fewest toys, and the common ratio of the geometric sequence is 1.5, find the number of toys the parent who leaves with the most toys takes home.

A history teacher, deeply inspired by Harriet Tubman's numerous journeys to free enslaved people via the Underground Railroad, decides to create a mathematical model to understand the logistics and risks involved in such missions. The teacher models each journey as a path on a weighted grid graph, where nodes represent safe houses, and edges represent the distance and risk associated with traveling between them.

1. Suppose the grid is a 5x5 matrix where each node (i, j) has a weight w_ij representing the risk factor, and each edge between nodes (i, j) and (i', j') has a distance d_ij_i'j'. The weight w_ij is given by the function w_ij = |i - 3| + |j - 3|, and the distance d_ij_i'j' between any two adjacent nodes is 1 unit. Calculate the shortest path in terms of total risk from the node representing the start point at (1, 1) to the node representing the endpoint at (5, 5), under the condition that the total distance traveled must not exceed 10 units.

2. Considering that each node's risk factor contributes to the overall probability of a successful mission, with the success probability being inversely proportional to the total risk encountered, formulate the probability function for a successful mission. Assume the success probability P is given by P = k / (1 + total risk), where k is a constant. Determine the constant k if the probability of success for a journey with a total risk of 10 is 0.5.

As a marketing manager for a sports apparel company specializing in Green Bay Packers merchandise, you have been tasked with optimizing the sales strategy for the upcoming football season. Your company has collected detailed sales data for the past five years, segmented by product category: jerseys, hats, and accessories. Assume the sales for each category can be modeled by the following polynomial functions, where \( t \) represents the number of years since the start of the data collection:

- Jerseys: \( J(t) = 300t^2 + 1500t + 2000 \)
- Hats: \( H(t) = -100t^2 + 800t + 1200 \)
- Accessories: \( A(t) = 50t^2 + 600t + 300 \)

1. Determine the year in which the total sales from all categories will reach their maximum value within a 5-year period. What are the total sales at this maximum point?

2. As part of a new campaign, your company plans to introduce a dynamic pricing model that adjusts prices based on predicted demand. Assuming the price elasticity of demand for jerseys is \( -1.2 \) and you plan to increase the price by 10%, calculate the expected change in quantity demanded for jerseys. Use the assumption that the current annual demand for jerseys is represented by the derivative of \( J(t) \) at \( t = 4 \).

John, a prideful older brother, always loves to showcase his math skills to his younger siblings. He decides to challenge them with a problem that involves a touch of number theory and calculus, areas in which he excels.

1. John asks his siblings to find all prime numbers \( p \) such that \( p^2 + 2 \) is also a prime number. 

2. After they struggle with the first part, he further challenges them by asking: Given a continuous function \( f(x) \) defined on the interval \([0, 2]\) such that \( f(0) = 1 \) and \( f(2) = 3 \), prove that there exists at least one \( c \in (0, 2) \) such that \( f'(c) = 1 \).

A think tank researcher is analyzing a welfare program designed to distribute funds among low-income households in a city. The city is divided into \( n \) districts, and each district \( i \) has a population \( p_i \) and a poverty rate \( r_i \) (expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1). The total budget available for distribution is \( B \).

1. Formulate the allocation of funds \( f_i \) to each district \( i \) such that the allocation is proportional to the product of the population and the poverty rate in each district. Ensure that the sum of all allocations does not exceed the total budget \( B \). Write the constraints and the objective function for this allocation problem.

2. After initial allocations, the researcher wants to evaluate the impact of the fund distribution on reducing poverty. They propose a model where the poverty rate in district \( i \) after receiving funds \( f_i \) is given by \( r_i' = r_i (1 - \frac{f_i}{m_i}) \), where \( m_i \) is a district-specific constant representing the amount of funds needed to completely eliminate poverty in that district. Derive the new overall poverty rate for the city after fund distribution and discuss any assumptions and limitations of this model.

A small business owner, Alex, has noticed that negative online reviews are affecting their brand image. They have collected data on the number of negative reviews received each month over the past year. The data shows that the number of negative reviews, \( N(t) \), can be modeled by the following function, where \( t \) is the month number (from 1 to 12):

\[ N(t) = 5 \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6} + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) + 8 \]

1. Calculate the total number of negative reviews Alex received over the year. 

2. Alex wants to reduce the impact of negative reviews by responding to them promptly. Suppose each response reduces the effect of a negative review by a factor of \( e^{-0.1r} \), where \( r \) is the number of responses. If Alex responds to each negative review exactly once, determine the total effective number of negative reviews for the entire year after considering the responses.

A social media influencer is tasked with promoting Taraji P. Henson's latest film project through various online platforms. The influencer aims to maximize audience engagement by strategically timing posts across these platforms. Assume the influencer has determined that the engagement (in terms of likes, comments, and shares) on a platform can be modeled by the function \( E(t) = A \cdot \sin(Bt + C) + D \), where \( E(t) \) represents the engagement at time \( t \) hours after the post is made, and \( A \), \( B \), \( C \), and \( D \) are constants determined from past data.

1. If the influencer makes a post at 1 PM and receives peak engagement at 4 PM, and the next peak occurs at 7 PM, determine the values of \( B \) and \( C \) given that \( A = 100 \) and \( D = 200 \).

2. Additionally, the influencer plans to post a behind-the-scenes video from Taraji P. Henson's project on a second platform where the engagement function is modeled by a different sinusoidal function \( F(t) = P \cdot \cos(Qt + R) + S \). Given that the maximum engagement on this second platform is 300 and occurs every 3 hours starting from when the post is made at 2 PM, find the possible values of \( Q \) and \( R \).

A sports bar owner has decided to revamp his business model to accommodate social distancing measures while maintaining the excitement of game-watching parties. He plans to set up multiple large screens and individual booths for patrons, each booth having a limited capacity due to social distancing.

1. Suppose the bar has a total area of 2000 square feet available for the booths and screens. Each booth requires 50 square feet, and each screen requires 20 square feet. Additionally, the bar owner wants to ensure that there is at least one screen for every four booths to provide optimal viewing experiences. Formulate a system of inequalities representing the number of booths \( b \) and screens \( s \) that can be set up, and determine the feasible region for \( b \) and \( s \).

2. To recreate the lively debates, the owner decides to host virtual trivia sessions. Each session can accommodate up to 10 online participants, and he plans to host 5 sessions per day. He estimates that each participant spends an average of $5 per session on food and drinks. Given a monthly goal of $7500 in revenue from these sessions, calculate the minimum number of days the owner needs to operate in a month to meet this goal, assuming all sessions are fully booked.

A charismatic rhetorician is preparing a speech to question the validity of logical positivism, and she decides to use a mathematical model to illustrate her argument. She constructs a complex emotional appeal based on the concept of Gödel's incompleteness theorems and the limitations of formal systems.

1. **Gödel's Incompleteness Theorem Application:** Consider a formal system \( S \) that is capable of encoding arithmetic. Let \( G(S) \) be a Gödel sentence for the system \( S \), which asserts its own unprovability within \( S \). Prove that if \( S \) is consistent, then \( G(S) \) is true but not provable within \( S \).

2. **Emotional Appeal through Chaos Theory:** To further her argument, she decides to illustrate the unpredictability of human emotions using a chaotic system. Consider the logistic map defined by the recurrence relation:
   
   \[
   x_{n+1} = r x_n (1 - x_n)
   \]
   
   where \( r \) is a parameter and \( 0 < x_n < 1 \). For \( r = 3.57 \), show that the system exhibits chaotic behavior by demonstrating that small changes in initial conditions \( x_0 \) lead to significantly different outcomes after a large number of iterations. Specifically, calculate the Lyapunov exponent \( \lambda \) for this system and show that \( \lambda > 0 \).

The rhetorician will use the results of these mathematical explorations to argue that both formal logical systems and human emotional responses are inherently limited and unpredictable, thus challenging the premise of logical positivism.

Consider a dedicated follower of Katherine Dimancescu's work who is deeply interested in genealogy and historical research. They decide to analyze a historical population dataset from the 17th century using advanced mathematical techniques.

1. Assume the population of a small town in New England during the 17th century grows according to the logistic growth model, given by the differential equation:
   \[
   \frac{dP}{dt} = rP \left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)
   \]
   where \(P(t)\) is the population at time \(t\), \(r\) is the intrinsic growth rate, and \(K\) is the carrying capacity. If the initial population \(P(0) = P_0\) is 100 individuals, the carrying capacity \(K\) is 1000 individuals, and the intrinsic growth rate \(r\) is 0.1 per year, find the population \(P(t)\) as a function of time \(t\).

2. Using the population model from sub-problem 1, determine the year in which the population reaches 90% of the carrying capacity. Calculate this time \(t\) in terms of years since the initial measurement.

Consider an AI nerd who loves reading about space, ocean, and intriguing animal species. 

Sub-problem 1: In a study of an exoplanet orbiting a distant star, astronomers have detected a potentially habitable ocean-covered planet. The planet has a perfectly spherical shape with a radius \( R \). The ocean's depth varies according to the function \( d(\theta, \phi) = R(1 + \epsilon \sin(\theta) \cos(\phi)) \), where \( \theta \) is the polar angle, \( \phi \) is the azimuthal angle, and \( \epsilon \) is a small constant representing the variation in depth. Derive an expression for the total volume of the ocean, \( V \), in terms of \( R \) and \( \epsilon \).

Sub-problem 2: On this exoplanet, a unique species of bioluminescent jellyfish has been discovered. The population density \( \rho(r) \) of these jellyfish at a distance \( r \) from the ocean surface follows an exponential decay model: \( \rho(r) = \rho_0 e^{-\lambda r} \), where \( \rho_0 \) is the density at the surface, and \( \lambda \) is a decay constant. Calculate the total population of these jellyfish in the ocean, assuming the ocean is uniformly mixed and extends from the surface to the depth given by \( d(\theta, \phi) \).

An experienced real estate agent in Amsterdam is analyzing the housing market in the city. She needs to provide an in-depth investment analysis for a new client interested in purchasing properties for rental income. The client is particularly interested in two different neighborhoods: De Pijp and Jordaan.

1. The agent has data indicating that the average annual rental yield in De Pijp is 5.2%, while in Jordaan it is 4.8%. The client has a budget of €3 million and wants to divide it between the two neighborhoods to maximize the total annual rental income. Let \( x \) represent the amount invested in De Pijp and \( y \) represent the amount invested in Jordaan. Formulate the optimization problem using these variables and determine the values of \( x \) and \( y \) that maximize the annual rental income.

2. Additionally, the agent knows that property prices in De Pijp are increasing at an average annual rate of 3.5%, and in Jordaan at a rate of 3.0%. If the client plans to sell the properties after 5 years, formulate an expression for the total value of the investments in both neighborhoods after 5 years. Use this expression to analyze whether the allocation strategy that maximizes annual rental income also maximizes the total value of the investments after 5 years.

A critical community member is analyzing the funding distribution of an educational trust to ensure transparency and fairness. The trust allocates funds to different schools based on a complex formula involving multiple variables, including student performance metrics, teacher-student ratios, and historical data on previous allocations.

1. The funding formula is given by the function \( F(x, y, z) = k \cdot (x^2 + \sqrt{y} + \ln(z+1)) \), where \( x \) represents the average student performance score (scaled from 0 to 100), \( y \) is the teacher-student ratio, \( z \) is the historical funding received (in millions of dollars), and \( k \) is a constant. Given that \( k = 2.5 \), \( x = 85 \), \( y = 30 \), and \( z = 1.5 \), calculate the total funding \( F \) allocated to a school.

2. To ensure transparency, the community member wants to compare the fairness of funding between two schools. If School A has an average student performance score of \( x_1 = 90 \), teacher-student ratio \( y_1 = 25 \), and historical funding \( z_1 = 2 \), and School B has an average student performance score of \( x_2 = 80 \), teacher-student ratio \( y_2 = 35 \), and historical funding \( z_2 = 1 \), compute the funding difference \( \Delta F = F_A - F_B \) between School A and School B, using the same function \( F(x, y, z) \) with \( k = 2.5 \).

An expatriate from Latvia wants to keep a connection with their homeland by reading articles from a Latvian cultural news website. The website posts articles at a random rate that follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of 3 articles per day. The expatriate plans to check the website once every 3 days. 

1. What is the probability that the expatriate will find exactly 7 new articles when they check the website after 3 days?

Additionally, the expatriate has a preference for reading articles on traditional Latvian folklore, which make up 40% of all articles posted on the website. 

2. Given that the expatriate finds exactly 7 new articles after 3 days, what is the probability that exactly 3 of these articles are about traditional Latvian folklore?

Blind Channel released an album containing 12 tracks, each with a distinct length. Suppose the lengths of these tracks (in minutes) form an arithmetic sequence. The sum of the lengths of the tracks is 90 minutes, and the length of the 6th track is equal to the average length of all tracks.

1. Find the common difference and the length of the first track in the arithmetic sequence.

2. If Blind Channel wants to increase the length of each track by a percentage such that the total length of the album becomes 108 minutes, what is the percentage increase for each track?

Principal Jane is designing a new curriculum for her high school students that integrates real-world applications into classroom instruction. She wants to create a project where students will use calculus and linear algebra to optimize the school’s energy consumption, based on various factors such as temperature, usage patterns, and energy costs.

1. The school’s daily energy consumption \( E(t) \) in kilowatt-hours (kWh) can be modeled by the function \( E(t) = 50 + 10\sin(\pi t / 12) \), where \( t \) is the time in hours from midnight (0 ≤ \( t \) ≤ 24). Calculate the total energy consumption of the school over a 24-hour period.

2. Additionally, Principal Jane wants to incorporate a linear algebra component where students must determine the optimal allocation of energy resources. The school has three main sections: classrooms, laboratories, and administrative offices. The energy requirements for each section can be represented as a system of linear equations:
   \[
   \begin{cases}
   2x + 3y + z = 300 \\
   x + 2y + 4z = 400 \\
   3x + y + 2z = 350 
   \end{cases}
   \]
   Solve for \( x \), \( y \), and \( z \), which represent the energy consumption in kWh for classrooms, laboratories, and administrative offices, respectively.

A charismatic bus driver, who knows every street and alley of the city like the back of his hand, embarks on a journey that involves telling stories to his passengers while navigating complex city routes. The city can be modeled as a grid of intersecting streets, where each intersection is a node and each block between intersections is a unit distance. The bus driver starts his route at the central node (0,0) of a 5x5 grid and plans to visit all the boundary nodes (nodes that lie on the perimeter of the grid) exactly once before returning to the starting point.

1. Considering each possible route as a permutation of the boundary nodes, calculate the total number of distinct routes the bus driver can take. Assume that the bus driver cannot revisit any node and must return to the starting point after visiting all boundary nodes once.

2. As the bus driver tells a story at each node, the duration of each story is modeled by a unique positive integer, such that the sum of all story durations equals the total distance traveled on the route (measured in unit distances). Given this constraint, devise a mathematical expression or formula for the sum of all possible story duration combinations that satisfy this condition, across all distinct routes.

A beauty product manufacturer collaborates with a hairstylist to develop a new line of hair care products. The effectiveness of the product is measured by a variable \( E(t) \), which represents the effectiveness as a function of time \( t \) in weeks. The effectiveness function is given by the differential equation:

\[ \frac{dE}{dt} = k(E - M) \]

where \( k \) is a constant representing the rate at which the product effectiveness changes, and \( M \) is the maximum effectiveness value. After conducting initial tests, the manufacturer and the hairstylist observe that the effectiveness of the product at \( t = 0 \) is \( E(0) = E_0 \).

Sub-problem 1:
Solve the differential equation for \( E(t) \) given the initial condition \( E(0) = E_0 \).

Sub-problem 2:
Assume the manufacturer wants the product to reach 90% of its maximum effectiveness \( M \) within 4 weeks. Determine the constant \( k \) that will satisfy this condition.

As a critical academic peer in the field of geography, you have been tasked with evaluating the accuracy of a new geospatial model which predicts the population density of a region based on various environmental factors. The model uses a combination of partial differential equations (PDEs) and statistical regression to estimate the population density function \( P(x, y) \) across a 2D plane where \( (x, y) \) represents geographical coordinates.

1. The population density function \( P(x, y) \) is given by the following PDE:
\[ \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial y^2} = -\lambda P \]
where \( \lambda \) is a positive constant representing the decay rate of population density due to natural and anthropogenic factors. Given the boundary conditions \( P(0, y) = P(a, y) = 0 \) and \( P(x, 0) = P(x, b) = 0 \) for a rectangular region \( 0 \leq x \leq a \) and \( 0 \leq y \leq b \), find the general solution for \( P(x, y) \).

2. To validate the model, you gather a sample dataset of observed population densities at specific coordinates within the region. The observed densities are \(\{P(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \). Using the least squares method, derive the expression for the best-fit constant \(\lambda\) that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the observed densities and the predicted densities from the general solution found in sub-problem 1.

A successful male tech mogul, Alex, known for his dismissive attitude about the skills and capabilities of women in tech, is developing a new algorithm to optimize cloud storage efficiency. He is challenged by his colleague, a highly skilled female data scientist named Clara, to solve the following problem:

1. Consider a cloud storage system where files are stored in a hierarchical tree structure. Each node in the tree represents a folder, and each edge represents a file. The root folder has a number of subfolders, each of which can also contain subfolders and files. If each file size is represented by an integer, create an algorithm to find the maximum file size difference between any two files within the same branch of the tree. Prove the time complexity of your algorithm.

2. Clara proposes an additional challenge to Alex. She suggests optimizing the storage by implementing a compression algorithm that reduces the size of files by a factor of \( f(i) = \frac{i}{\log(i+1)} \), where \( i \) is the original file size. Given the original file sizes \( \{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n\} \) in one of the subfolders, calculate the total storage saved after applying the compression algorithm to all files in that subfolder. Show your steps and justify your method.

Can Alex prove his proficiency and solve these problems, or will Clara's challenge expose the gaps in his dismissive attitude?

As a home interior designer with a passion for sophisticated and stylish items, you have been tasked with designing a unique, modern chandelier for a luxury penthouse. The chandelier will be composed of a series of geometric shapes that incorporate both aesthetics and functionality.

1. The chandelier is to be constructed from n identical tetrahedral modules. Each module is made from a material that has a density of ρ kg/m³ and edges of length a meters. The modules are arranged to form a larger, regular polyhedron, specifically a truncated icosahedron, which is also known as a soccer ball shape and consists of 12 regular pentagonal faces and 20 regular hexagonal faces. Determine the total mass of the chandelier if the material for each module is uniformly dense.

2. To enhance the sophistication, the interior of each tetrahedral module is designed to house a stylish LED light that emits light uniformly in all directions. The light intensity diminishes with the square of the distance from the source. If the chandelier is suspended at a height h meters above a circular dining table with radius r meters, find the total illumination intensity at the center of the table, assuming that each LED has an initial intensity of I₀ lumens at a distance of 1 meter. Consider the effect of overlapping light from multiple modules.

Your cousin, who is a skilled gamer, frequently challenges you to friendly competitions. In one such game, you both decide to play a strategy game that involves collecting resources and building structures. The game has the following rules:

1. Each player starts with zero resources.
2. In each round, a player can either gather resources or build a structure. 
3. Gathering resources gives a player \(2^n\) resources where \(n\) is the number of the round.
4. Building a structure requires \(k \times 2^m\) resources, where \(k\) is a constant and \(m\) is the number of the round in which the structure is built.

Assume you and your cousin play for \(N\) rounds and you both gather resources in every round except the last one, where you both build a structure.

Sub-problems:

1. Determine the total number of resources each player has gathered by the end of round \(N-1\).
2. If the constant \(k=3\), find the minimum number of rounds \(N\) required for both you and your cousin to have just enough resources to build the structure in the final round.

An independent filmmaker, inspired by Wes Craven's work, decides to create a horror movie series. The filmmaker plans to incorporate elements of suspense and surprise by using a probabilistic model to determine the timing of key scare moments, which they refer to as "scare nodes," throughout the movie.

Sub-problem 1:
The filmmaker models the timing of these scare nodes using a Poisson process, where the average rate of scare nodes is 3 per hour. If the movie is 90 minutes long, what is the probability that there will be exactly 4 scare nodes in the film?

Sub-problem 2:
In addition to the Poisson process, the filmmaker uses a geometric distribution to determine the sequence of scenes leading up to a scare node. If the probability of transitioning from a suspense scene to a scare node in any given scene is 0.2, what is the expected number of suspense scenes before a scare node occurs? 

Consider these factors and calculate the resulting probabilities and expectations to aid the filmmaker in crafting a perfectly timed horror experience.

A single mother, Sarah, is advocating for her son's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) and is analyzing the effectiveness of different educational strategies to improve her son's academic performance in mathematics. She has collected data over several months on how different types of instructional time allocation impact his learning outcomes. 

1. Sarah wants to find the optimal allocation of instructional time between two strategies: direct instruction (x hours per week) and exploratory learning (y hours per week). Her observations suggest that the improvement in her son's math scores, I(x, y), can be modeled by the function:

   \[ I(x, y) = 3x^2 + 4y^2 - xy + 6x + 8y - 100 \]

   where \( x + y = 10 \). Determine the values of \( x \) and \( y \) that maximize the improvement function \( I(x, y) \).

2. Based on the optimal values found in sub-problem 1, Sarah wants to further refine the strategies by introducing a new parameter \( z \), representing the time spent in collaborative learning with peers. She hypothesizes that including this parameter will enhance the model. The new improvement function is given by:

   \[ J(x, y, z) = 3x^2 + 4y^2 + 5z^2 - xy - xz - yz + 6x + 8y + 10z - 150 \]

   with the constraint \( x + y + z = 15 \). Find the values of \( x \), \( y \), and \( z \) that maximize \( J(x, y, z) \).

An apprentice is learning the craft of ceramics from an artist and assisting with various tasks. One of the tasks involves creating ceramic vases where the shape of the vase is defined by rotating a curve around the y-axis. The curve follows the equation \( y = kx^3 \) for \( 0 \leq x \leq a \), where \( k \) and \( a \) are constants determined by the artist.

1. The apprentice needs to calculate the volume of the vase generated by rotating the curve \( y = kx^3 \) around the y-axis. Express the volume \( V \) as an integral and find \( V \) in terms of \( k \) and \( a \).

2. The artist wants the vase to have a specific surface area. The apprentice must find the total surface area \( S \) of the vase, excluding the top circular opening, when the vase is rotated around the y-axis. Express the surface area \( S \) as an integral and find \( S \) in terms of \( k \) and \( a \).

A concerned parent in a community with a population of 50,000 wants to analyze the impact of violent crime on family stability. They gather the following data:

1. The rate of violent crimes in the community is 5 per 1,000 people annually.
2. Each violent crime affects an average of 3 family units.
3. The probability that a family will move out of the community within a year after being affected by a violent crime is 0.25.

Sub-problems:

1. Calculate the expected number of family units affected by violent crimes in one year.
2. Determine the expected number of family units that will move out of the community within a year due to violent crimes.

Use these values to understand the overall impact on the community and develop a strategy to mitigate the family displacement.

Dr. Emily, an NHS medical professional, is analyzing the engagement scores and diversity index of her hospital departments. She values employee engagement and diversity, and she believes that both factors are interrelated and can be modeled mathematically. 

1. **Engagement Scores Analysis:** The engagement scores of the departments follow a normal distribution with a mean of 75 and a standard deviation of 10. If Dr. Emily wants to identify the top 10% of departments in terms of engagement scores, what is the minimum engagement score a department must have to be in the top 10%?

2. **Diversity Index Analysis:** Dr. Emily measures the diversity index of each department using an index \( D \) that is defined as \( D = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+x_i} \), where \( n \) is the number of employees in the department and \( x_i \) is the number of years each employee has been with the NHS. Suppose there are 20 departments each with 15 employees, and the years with the NHS for these employees range uniformly from 1 to 30 years. Calculate the average diversity index \( \bar{D} \) for these 20 departments. 

Note: The uniform distribution implies that the number of years \( x_i \) are uniformly distributed between 1 and 30.

As an artist and musician influenced by XXXTentacion, you decide to create a conceptual piece that combines both visual art and music. You want to encode one of XXXTentacion's songs into a visual pattern using a mathematical transformation.

1. Suppose you want to represent the audio waveform of a 4-minute-long song as a continuous function \( f(t) \), where \( t \) is time in seconds and \( f(t) \) represents the amplitude of the audio signal at time \( t \). Let \( f(t) \) be sampled at a rate of 44.1 kHz (44,100 samples per second). Define the Fourier Transform \( \mathcal{F}(f(t)) \) of this function and determine the frequency domain representation \( \hat{f}(\omega) \). Describe the process and provide the general form of \( \hat{f}(\omega) \).

2. Using the Fourier series coefficients obtained, you decide to create a visual art piece where the intensity of the color at a point \( (x, y) \) on a canvas is given by a function \( I(x, y) \), which is a combination of selected coefficients. If the canvas is a unit square \( [0,1] \times [0,1] \), and the intensity function is given by:

\[ I(x, y) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} |\hat{f}(k \cdot \omega_0)| \cdot \cos(2\pi k (x+y)) \]

where \( \omega_0 \) is a fundamental frequency and \( N \) is the number of significant Fourier coefficients. Explain how you would determine the value of \( N \) and \( \omega_0 \) from the Fourier Transform of the audio signal and describe the expected pattern on the canvas.

A representative from the local Small Business Administration office is assisting a small business owner with their financial planning. The business owner is considering applying for a combination of a grant and a loan to expand their operations. The total amount they wish to secure is $150,000. The grant covers 40% of the total amount needed, and the loan will cover the remaining 60%. The loan has an interest rate of 5% per annum, compounded annually, and must be repaid over 5 years.

1. Calculate the amount of money the business owner will receive from the grant and the amount they will need to borrow through the loan.

2. Determine the total amount the business owner will have to repay on the loan after 5 years, including interest.

Marcia, a middle-aged woman living in Jamaica, is deeply involved in her local community. She runs a community center that offers a variety of classes, including math tutoring, fitness classes, and art workshops. The community center is funded by donations and a small fee for each class.

1. The community center offers a math tutoring class twice a week, and each class is attended by an average of 12 students. To maintain a high-quality learning environment, Marcia wants to ensure that the student-to-tutor ratio does not exceed 4:1. If Marcia currently has 3 tutors available, calculate the maximum number of additional students she can accommodate per week without hiring more tutors. 

2. The community center also hosts a weekly fitness event on Saturdays, which is attended by an average of 50 community members. Each attendee pays a fee of JMD 200, and the total expenses for hosting the event amount to JMD 6,000. Marcia plans to use the net proceeds from these events to fund the purchase of new equipment for the art workshops. If the cost of the new equipment is JMD 50,000, determine the minimum number of fitness events Marcia needs to host to cover the cost of the equipment.

A startup founder is planning to build a scalable data infrastructure that will handle large volumes of data efficiently. The infrastructure relies on a distributed database system that uses a sharding technique to distribute data across multiple servers. Each server can handle a maximum of \( \lambda \) queries per second.

1. The founder aims to ensure that the system can handle a peak load of \( N \) queries per second. If each server can handle up to \( \lambda \) queries per second, and the data is uniformly distributed, determine the minimum number of servers \( S \) required to maintain this peak load. Express \( S \) in terms of \( N \) and \( \lambda \).

2. In addition to handling the peak load, the founder wants to optimize the data retrieval time by minimizing the communication overhead between servers. The probability of a query needing data from more than one server follows a Poisson distribution with rate parameter \( \mu \). Formulate an expression for the expected number of queries requiring inter-server communication per second and discuss the impact of increasing \( \mu \) on the system's overall performance and scalability.

Dr. Elara Simmons, a biochemist specializing in alternative testing methods that do not involve animals, is modeling the growth dynamics of a cell culture used to test a new drug. The cell culture grows according to a logistic growth model, given by the differential equation:

\[ \frac{dN}{dt} = rN \left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right) \]

where \( N(t) \) is the population of cells at time \( t \), \( r \) is the growth rate, and \( K \) is the carrying capacity of the culture.

Sub-problem 1: If Dr. Simmons starts with an initial cell population \( N(0) = N_0 \), derive the explicit solution \( N(t) \) for the logistic growth equation in terms of \( N_0 \), \( r \), and \( K \).

Sub-problem 2: Dr. Simmons observes that the cell population reaches half of the carrying capacity (\( K/2 \)) at time \( t = T \). Given the parameters \( r = 0.1 \) days\(^{-1}\), \( K = 10^6 \) cells, and \( N_0 = 10^3 \) cells, determine the time \( T \) when the cell population reaches \( K/2 \).

A high school student, Alex, is preparing for the SAT and wants to maximize their study time effectively. Alex has decided to allocate a specific number of hours each week to study for the math section. To test their understanding of functions and sequences, consider the following problem:

1. Alex notices that their study efficiency follows a pattern. The number of math problems Alex can solve in a week, \( P(n) \), is modeled by a quadratic function \( P(n) = an^2 + bn + c \), where \( n \) is the number of weeks since Alex started studying. In the first week, Alex solved 10 problems, in the second week, 18 problems, and in the third week, 30 problems. Determine the values of \( a \), \( b \), and \( c \).

2. Based on the function \( P(n) \) obtained in part 1, Alex aims to solve at least 100 problems in a particular week to feel confident for the SAT. Determine the minimum number of weeks, \( n \), it will take Alex to achieve this goal.

A project manager is overseeing a software development project that involves both theoretical algorithm analysis and practical implementation. The project manager needs to optimize the project's timeline and resource allocation to balance theoretical research and practical coding.

1. Theoretical research involves analyzing an algorithm with a complexity of \(O(n^2 \log n)\). If the project manager allocates \(T\) hours for theoretical research, where \(T\) is a function of the input size \(n\) given by \(T(n) = k \cdot n^2 \log n\), and \(k\) is a constant. Determine the value of \(T\) for \(n = 1024\) and \(k = 0.5\).

2. Practical implementation involves writing and debugging code, which can be modeled by a function \(P(n) = m \cdot n \log n + c\), where \(m\) and \(c\) are constants. Given that for \(n = 1024\), \(P(1024) = 20480\) and for \(n = 512\), \(P(512) = 8960\), find the values of \(m\) and \(c\).

The project manager must ensure that the combined time for theoretical research and practical implementation does not exceed 30000 hours for \(n = 1024\). Verify if the combined time for \(n = 1024\) meets this requirement.

A UK local farmer grows three types of crops: wheat, barley, and oats. The farmer has a total of 100 hectares of land. Due to the local market demand and crop rotation practices, the farmer needs to allocate the land such that:

1. The area allocated to barley should be at least twice the area allocated to oats.
2. The combined area for wheat and barley should not exceed 80 hectares.
3. The profit from each hectare of wheat, barley, and oats are £500, £300, and £400 respectively.

Given these constraints, the farmer wants to maximize his profit. 

1. Formulate this problem as a linear programming model. Define the variables, the objective function, and the constraints.
2. Solve the linear programming model using the simplex method or any other appropriate algorithm to find the optimal land allocation for wheat, barley, and oats to maximize the farmer's profit.

A radio news anchor operates a station that broadcasts news updates in between musical segments. The anchor has a schedule where each hour consists of 15 minutes of news updates and 45 minutes of music. The news updates are broken into multiple segments, and the anchor wants to optimize the schedule to maximize listener engagement.

1. If the news update segments can only be in increments of 5 minutes and must be equally spaced throughout the hour, determine the number of different scheduling arrangements possible for the news segments within an hour. Assume that no two news segments can be adjacent to each other.

2. Consider that the radio station tracks the effectiveness of news updates by measuring the listener engagement, which follows a sinusoidal pattern given by \( E(t) = A \sin(\omega t + \phi) + B \), where \( E(t) \) is the engagement at time \( t \) in minutes past the hour, \( A \), \( \omega \), \( \phi \), and \( B \) are constants. If listener engagement peaks every 20 minutes and the maximum engagement is double the average engagement, find the values of \( \omega \) and \( A \) given that the average engagement is 50 units.

A group of educators and historians are curating a special exhibit on ancient civilizations, focusing on the time periods and cultural contexts of Ancient Egypt and Ancient Greece. They have discovered a rectangular stone tablet from Ancient Egypt with dimensions \(a\) and \(b\), and a circular mosaic from Ancient Greece with radius \(r\).

1. The stone tablet is inscribed with hieroglyphics that form a repeating pattern. The area covered by one repeating unit of the pattern is given by the quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), where \(a, b,\) and \(c\) are integers representing certain historical constants. If the roots of this equation are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), express the sum and product of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) in terms of the dimensions \(a\) and \(b\) of the stone tablet. Then, determine the possible values of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) given that the area of the stone tablet is \(60 \, \text{square units}\) and the roots must be positive integers.

2. The circular mosaic contains intricate geometric patterns, and the historians have determined that the total area of the patterns is exactly half the area of the circle. Given that the radius \(r\) of the mosaic is an integer and using the value of \(\pi\), find the radius \(r\) such that the area of the patterns is equal to the product of the roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) from sub-problem 1.

As a curator at a Holocaust museum, you are tasked with preserving and displaying survivor's personal stories and sacred family heirlooms. You decide to create an exhibit that includes a digital interactive timeline and a physical display of heirlooms. 

1. For the digital timeline, each survivor's story is represented by a unique polynomial function \( P_i(t) \), where \( t \) is the time in years since the end of World War II (1945). The interactive timeline will display the stories in a way that no two stories intersect on the timeline for the first 100 years after 1945. Given that \( P_i(t) = a_i t^3 + b_i t^2 + c_i t + d_i \) for survivor \( i \), derive the conditions on the coefficients \( a_i \), \( b_i \), \( c_i \), and \( d_i \) that ensure the functions \( P_i(t) \) and \( P_j(t) \) for any \( i \neq j \) do not intersect for \( t \) in the interval [0, 100].

2. For the physical display of heirlooms, you are given a collection of items with varying dimensions that need to fit into a display case with a fixed volume \( V \). The shape of the display case is a rectangular prism with dimensions \( x \), \( y \), and \( z \), and the total surface area available for display is \( A \). Formulate and solve the optimization problem to determine the dimensions \( x \), \( y \), and \( z \) of the display case that maximize the surface area \( A \) given the volume constraint \( V \).

A retired mechanical engineer, who spent decades designing gears and mechanical systems, recalls the intricate balance of forces and rotational dynamics that made traditional machines so efficient. Consider a mechanical system consisting of two interconnected gears, Gear A and Gear B, with the following characteristics:

1. Gear A has a radius of \( r_A = 15 \) cm and Gear B has a radius of \( r_B = 45 \) cm. The gears are in perfect contact and rotate without slipping. If Gear A rotates at an angular speed of \( \omega_A = 120 \) radians per second, determine the angular speed \( \omega_B \) of Gear B.

2. In addition to rotational dynamics, the engineer also recalls the importance of balancing forces in mechanical systems. Suppose Gear A is subjected to a tangential force of \( F_A = 200 \) N at its edge. Assuming that the system is in equilibrium, calculate the tangential force \( F_B \) exerted at the edge of Gear B. Consider that the moment of inertia of Gear B is \( I_B = 0.5 \times m_B \times r_B^2 \), where \( m_B \) is the mass of Gear B, and that Gear B does not experience any angular acceleration. 

Solve these problems, considering the laws of rotational dynamics and the principle of mechanical advantage in gear systems.

As a Tasmanian ecologist focusing on endangered plant species, you are tasked with monitoring a specific endangered plant population in a protected reserve. The population dynamics of this plant can be modeled by the following logistic differential equation:

\[
\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - h(t)
\]

where \( P(t) \) is the plant population size at time \( t \), \( r \) is the intrinsic growth rate, \( K \) is the carrying capacity of the environment, and \( h(t) \) is a time-dependent harvesting function representing the effects of environmental threats such as invasive species or human interference.

1. Suppose the intrinsic growth rate \( r = 0.05 \), the carrying capacity \( K = 1000 \), and the harvesting function is \( h(t) = 20\sin(\frac{\pi}{6} t) \). Determine the equilibrium solutions of the differential equation and analyze their stability.

2. Assume that due to conservation efforts, the harvesting function \( h(t) \) is modified to a constant \( h_0 \) such that \( h_0 < rK \). Determine the critical value of \( h_0 \) that ensures the long-term survival of the plant population, given that the population must remain above 50% of the carrying capacity to be considered viable.

Sunita Baral, a renowned mathematician, has a dedicated supporter who admires her work on complex number theory and graph theory. Inspired by her latest research, the supporter decides to solve a challenging problem that combines both fields.

Consider the following complex numbers:
\[ z_1 = 3 + 4i \]
\[ z_2 = 1 - 2i \]

1. Calculate the product \( z_1 \cdot z_2 \) and represent it in the form \( a + bi \).

2. Sunita Baral proposes a graph \( G \) where each vertex represents a complex number \( z \) in the form \( a + bi \) (with \( a, b \in \mathbb{Z} \)), and an edge exists between two vertices \( z_1 \) and \( z_2 \) if and only if \( |z_1 - z_2| = k \) for a fixed integer \( k \). The supporter wants to determine the smallest \( k \) such that the graph \( G \) is connected when considering the vertices corresponding to the complex numbers \( z_1 \) and \( z_2 \) as defined above.

An entrepreneur has accumulated a wealth of $50 million, which they plan to distribute among their three children according to specific inheritance laws. The laws state that any estate worth over $20 million is subject to a 40% estate tax, but there is a provision that allows for a tax-free transfer of up to $15 million distributed across all beneficiaries. The entrepreneur is considering setting up a trust to minimize the tax burden and ensure a fair distribution among their children, but the trust incurs a setup cost of $1 million.

1. If the entrepreneur decides not to set up a trust and distributes the estate directly, how much will each child receive after taxes, assuming they want to distribute the estate equally among the three children?

2. If the entrepreneur sets up the trust, calculate the optimal distribution strategy that minimizes the tax burden and maximizes the post-tax inheritance for each child, taking into account the trust setup cost.

A dietitian is tasked with adapting a traditional lasagna recipe to accommodate both a low-carb and high-protein diet while ensuring that the dish remains flavorful and nutritious. The original recipe calls for a pasta layer containing 40% carbohydrates by weight, a meat layer with 15% protein by weight, and a cheese layer with 25% fat by weight. The goal is to reduce the total carbohydrate content by 50% and increase the protein content by 30% without altering the total weight of each layer.

1. Determine the new carbohydrate percentage in the pasta layer if it is to be replaced by an alternative ingredient that maintains the total weight of the layer but reduces carbohydrates by 50%. Assume that all other nutritional content remains constant. Provide the mathematical expression for the percentage of carbohydrates in the new pasta layer.

2. If the original meat layer weighs 500 grams, calculate the necessary increase in weight of a protein-rich substitute (which contains 30% protein by weight) to achieve the desired 30% increase in total protein content from the meat layer alone. What will be the new weight of the protein-rich substitute layer?

A distinguished science professor, known for their expertise in quantum mechanics and a penchant for recommending intriguing science literature, decides to explore the mathematical underpinnings of a concept featured in one of their suggested books: the Many-Worlds Interpretation of quantum mechanics. This interpretation suggests that all possible alternate histories and futures are real, each representing an actual "world" or "universe."

1. Consider a quantum system described by a wave function \( \psi(x, t) \), which evolves over time according to the Schrödinger equation. The professor is interested in a particular observable \( \hat{A} \) with eigenvalues \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \). Suppose the wave function can be expressed as a linear combination of the eigenfunctions \( \phi_1, \phi_2, \ldots, \phi_n \) of \( \hat{A} \) at a specific time \( t_0 \): 
   \[
   \psi(x, t_0) = c_1 \phi_1(x) + c_2 \phi_2(x) + \ldots + c_n \phi_n(x)
   \]
   where \( c_i \) are complex coefficients. Determine the probability \( P(a_i) \) of measuring the eigenvalue \( a_i \) at time \( t_0 \).

2. To further delve into the Many-Worlds concept, the professor postulates a scenario where each possible measurement outcome corresponds to a "branch" in the universe. Assuming \( n \) distinct measurement outcomes, calculate the number of distinct branching sequences over \( k \) consecutive measurements, assuming each measurement outcome is independent of the previous ones. Consider the complexity of managing these branches and estimate the growth rate of the number of branches as \( k \) increases, providing insight into the computational challenges faced in simulating such a multiverse scenario.

An avid listener tunes into a podcast every day to learn about different topics. The podcast releases an episode daily, and each episode has a duration that follows a normal distribution. The mean duration of an episode is 45 minutes with a standard deviation of 10 minutes.

1. Given that the listener plans to listen to the podcast for the next 30 days, what is the probability that the average duration of the episodes over these 30 days will be between 43 and 47 minutes?

2. Suppose the listener wants to maximize learning by ensuring they listen to at least 80% of the total content released over the next 60 days. If they can only spare a fixed number of minutes each day to listen, how many minutes per day should they allocate to achieve this goal, given the same normal distribution of episode durations?

Note: Use appropriate statistical methods and concepts to solve the problem, including the Central Limit Theorem, probability theory, and normal distribution properties.

As an odds analyst, you are tasked with predicting the outcomes of various sports matches to attract more followers. You decide to use a combination of historical data and Bayesian statistics to refine your predictions. You have been analyzing the performance of a certain football team, and you have the following data:

- The team has played 20 games in the current season.
- They won 12 games and lost 8 games.
- Historically, this team wins 60% of their games over the last 5 years.

1. Using Bayesian statistics, compute the posterior probability that the team will win their next game, given the prior historical win rate and the current season's performance. Assume a Beta distribution as a conjugate prior with parameters α (successes) and β (failures), where α and β are based on the historical win rate over the last 5 years (assume 100 games per season).

2. Once you have calculated the posterior probability, you decide to improve your model by incorporating a new variable: the team's win rate against their next opponent, which is 70% over the last 10 encounters. Using this information, update your posterior probability to reflect this additional factor. Consider this variable as a multiplicative factor to the posterior probability obtained in the first sub-problem.

A retired military officer who served in the Saudi Arabian Armed Forces is now involved in strategic military planning consultancy. He needs to optimize the placement of radar stations to ensure maximum coverage of a critical area in the desert, which is modeled as a 2D plane. The area of interest is represented as a polygon with vertices at the following coordinates: (2,3), (4,8), (7,5), (6,1), and (3,2). The radar stations have a circular coverage area with a radius of 3 units.

1. Determine the minimum number of radar stations needed to cover the entire area of the polygon. Use advanced geometric algorithms and optimization techniques to solve this problem.

2. Calculate the optimal coordinates for placing these radar stations to ensure complete coverage while minimizing redundancy. Use concepts from computational geometry and linear programming to determine these coordinates.

A vintage fabric seller, Alex, sources unique fabrics for content creators' projects. Alex has a collection of fabrics from various eras, and each fabric piece is characterized by its unique pattern and color scheme. Alex measures the uniqueness of a fabric using a score that combines the rarity of its pattern (P) and the distinctiveness of its color scheme (C) using the function \( U(P, C) = aP^2 + bC^3 \), where \( a \) and \( b \) are constants that depend on market trends.

1. Alex has found a fabric with a pattern rarity score of 4 and a color distinctiveness score of 3. Given that \( a = 2 \) and \( b = 1.5 \), calculate the uniqueness score of this fabric.

2. To optimize the selection of fabrics, Alex wants to maximize the uniqueness score function \( U(P, C) = 2P^2 + 1.5C^3 \) subject to the constraint \( 3P + 2C = 18 \). Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the values of \( P \) and \( C \) that maximize the uniqueness score.

As a biased alumnus who cherishes the legacy of the 1975 Davidson Wildcats football team, you believe their performance in a hypothetical season was unparalleled. Assume that the team played a total of \( n \) games, each game against a different team, and each game could either be a win, loss, or draw. The biased alumnus insists that the team's performance was such that the probabilities of winning, losing, and drawing any given game were all distinct prime numbers over the interval \([0,1]\).

1. Calculate the number of possible combinations of win-loss-draw records for the Davidson Wildcats if the sum of the probabilities of any outcome (win, loss, draw) is equal to 1, and each probability is a distinct prime number over the interval \([0,1]\). Assume \( n = 10 \).

2. Given that the biased alumnus fervently believes that the probability of the team winning a game was the greatest among all outcomes, determine the number of games the Wildcats were expected to win in this hypothetical season.

A software developer is tasked with creating a predictive model for the price of Bitcoin using the Coinbase API, despite having no prior experience with Bitcoin or the API. The developer decides to use a simplified mathematical model to understand the price dynamics before diving into the API.

1. **Time-Series Analysis**: Suppose the developer collects the daily closing prices of Bitcoin for the past 100 days, represented as \( \{P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_{100}\} \). They want to fit a linear regression model of the form \( P_t = \alpha t + \beta \) to approximate the trend of Bitcoin prices over time. Determine the values of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) using the least squares method.

2. **Predictive Model**: After fitting the linear regression model, the developer realizes that Bitcoin prices exhibit significant volatility and decides to incorporate a stochastic component. Assume \( \epsilon_t \) is a white noise term with zero mean and constant variance \( \sigma^2 \). Modify the linear regression model to include this stochastic term, resulting in \( P_t = \alpha t + \beta + \epsilon_t \). Suppose the developer wants to predict the price \( P_{101} \) using this model. Calculate the expected value and variance of \( P_{101} \).

A government official responsible for preserving cultural heritage is working with a linguist to translate a collection of historical documents. These documents are written in an ancient language with a unique set of symbols. The linguist has identified that each symbol can be represented by a unique prime number, and the translation requires determining the numerical value of each document by summing the prime numbers associated with its symbols. 

1. Suppose there are 10 different symbols used across the collection, with the smallest prime number assigned being 2 and the largest being 31. The sequence of prime numbers assigned is strictly increasing. Calculate the total sum of all prime numbers assigned to the symbols.

2. The linguist needs to verify the authenticity of a particular document by checking if the sum of the prime numbers of its symbols is a prime number itself. If a document contains symbols represented by the prime numbers {3, 5, 11, 17}, determine whether the sum of these primes is a prime number. If not, provide a prime factorization of the sum.

A street artist is creating a mural on a wall that incorporates elements of local history. The wall is a rectangular plane, and the artist wants to use a design that features a Fibonacci spiral, which is often seen as a symbol of growth and harmony, reflecting the city's development over time. The spiral is inscribed within a golden rectangle, which itself is part of a larger artistic composition that takes up the entire wall.

1. The wall dimensions are given as a width of 21 meters and a height of 34 meters, forming a golden rectangle. The artist decides to start the Fibonacci spiral from a square of side 1 meter located at the bottom left corner of the wall. Determine the exact number of full squares of Fibonacci dimensions (1 meter, 1 meter, 2 meters, 3 meters, etc.) that can fit within the wall, and calculate the total area covered by these squares.

2. To further incorporate historical elements, the artist decides to overlay a pattern of circles representing key historical events of the city. Each circle has a radius that is a Fibonacci number in meters, starting with a radius of 1 meter. The centers of these circles are placed at the corners of each square used to construct the Fibonacci spiral. Calculate the total area of the wall that is covered by at least one circle, assuming no two circles overlap.

As a market analyst with an optimistic outlook, you have been tasked with evaluating the future performance of a company whose stock has shown consistent growth. You have historical quarterly revenue data for the past 5 years, which fits a logistic growth model due to market saturation concerns. The revenue \( R(t) \) (in millions of dollars) as a function of time \( t \) (in quarters) is modeled by the equation:

\[ R(t) = \frac{L}{1 + e^{-k(t - t_0)}} \]

where \( L \) is the maximum potential revenue, \( k \) is the growth rate, and \( t_0 \) is the inflection point (the quarter at which the company achieves half of its maximum potential revenue).

1. Given the data points: \( R(0) = 10 \), \( R(4) = 20 \), \( R(8) = 35 \), and \( R(12) = 50 \), estimate the parameters \( L \), \( k \), and \( t_0 \) using a non-linear regression method. Assume the data is perfectly fit by the model.

2. Once you have estimated the parameters, forecast the revenue for the next 8 quarters (i.e., from \( t = 13 \) to \( t = 20 \)). Considering your positive outlook, calculate the probability that the revenue will exceed 80% of the maximum potential revenue \( L \) by quarter 20. Assume any deviations from the model follow a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 2 million dollars.

A computer science student is designing an automated system that uses machine learning to optimize the energy consumption of a data center. The data center consists of \( n \) servers, each with a distinct energy consumption profile. The student models the energy consumption of each server as a continuous function \( f_i(t) \), where \( t \) is the time in hours, and \( i \) is the server index, \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \).

1. Given that the total energy consumption \( E(t) \) of the data center at time \( t \) is expressed as:
   \[
   E(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(t) + A \cdot \int_{0}^{t} \sum_{i=1}^{n} g_i(s) \, ds
   \]
   where \( A \) is a constant coefficient and \( g_i(s) \) is a function representing the potential savings from automation at server \( i \) over time \( s \), derive a general expression for the rate of change of total energy consumption with respect to time, \( \frac{dE}{dt} \).

2. Assume that the goal of the automated system is to minimize the total energy consumption over a 24-hour period. Formulate and solve a constrained optimization problem using the Lagrange multipliers method, where the constraint is that the total potential savings from automation across all servers cannot exceed a fixed value \( S \):
   \[
   \int_{0}^{24} \sum_{i=1}^{n} g_i(t) \, dt \leq S
   \]
   Provide the conditions under which the optimization problem has a unique solution.

Consider a simplified model of a microprocessor that uses a binary number system for computation. The microprocessor's architecture can be represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where each node represents a computational unit capable of performing a basic arithmetic operation (addition or multiplication), and each directed edge represents the flow of binary data between units.

Sub-problem 1:
Assume the DAG of the microprocessor has \( n \) nodes and \( m \) directed edges. The binary data flowing through the DAG is represented by \( k \)-bit binary numbers. Design an algorithm to determine the maximum bit-length of the output produced by the DAG when each node performs an operation on its inputs, considering potential overflow. Show that your algorithm runs in \( O(n + m) \) time.

Sub-problem 2:
Suppose two specific nodes in the DAG, \( A \) and \( B \), are known to frequently perform computations on data from the same source node \( S \). Given that the computational cost between two nodes is proportional to the Hamming distance between their output binary numbers, derive an expression for the expected computational cost between nodes \( A \) and \( B \). Assume each bit in the binary numbers is equally likely to be 0 or 1 and that the operations performed by \( A \) and \( B \) are independent.

A nurse is conducting a study to determine the effectiveness of Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) combined with counseling sessions on patients who are trying to quit smoking. The study tracks 100 patients over a period of 12 months. The patients are divided into two groups: Group A (NRT + counseling) and Group B (NRT only). The nurse collects data on the number of cigarettes smoked per day by each patient at the start of the study and at the end of each month. The data for the number of cigarettes smoked per day follows a normal distribution.

Sub-problem 1:
Given that the mean reduction in the number of cigarettes smoked per day for Group A after 12 months is 15 with a standard deviation of 4, and for Group B, the mean reduction is 10 with a standard deviation of 5, perform a hypothesis test at a 0.05 significance level to determine if the difference in mean reductions between the two groups is statistically significant.

Sub-problem 2:
The nurse wants to create a predictive model to estimate the probability that a randomly selected patient from Group A will reduce their cigarette consumption by at least 20 cigarettes per day after 12 months. Assume the reduction in cigarettes per day for Group A follows a normal distribution. Calculate this probability.

The grandchild, who identifies as non-binary, decides to host a weekly discussion group about gender identity and acceptance. They want to analyze the dynamics of conversation and representation over time using a model involving advanced mathematics.

1. The group starts with an initial number of participants, \( P_0 \), which includes equal representation of non-binary, male, and female participants. The non-binary grandchild notices that each week, the number of participants increases by a percentage that models acceptance and awareness growth, \( r(t) = 0.05 \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right) + 0.03 \), where \( t \) is the number of weeks since the group started. Formulate a differential equation that models the growth of the group over time, and solve for the number of participants \( P(t) \) after \( t \) weeks, given that \( P_0 = 30 \).

2. In the same discussion group, the grandchild wants to ensure that the conversation is balanced. They model the balance using an entropy function \( H(t) = -\sum_{i=1}^{3} p_i(t) \log(p_i(t)) \), where \( p_1(t) \), \( p_2(t) \), and \( p_3(t) \) represent the proportions of non-binary, male, and female participants, respectively. Assuming that these proportions change as \( p_1(t) = \frac{1}{3} + 0.1 \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right) \), \( p_2(t) = \frac{1}{3} - 0.05 \cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right) \), and \( p_3(t) = 1 - p_1(t) - p_2(t) \), calculate the entropy \( H(t) \) at \( t = 12 \) weeks.

A former patient of the psychiatrist is haunted by the controversial treatments that were administered. One of the treatments involved sessions where complex patterns of light and sound were used to induce certain brainwave activities. The patient, in an attempt to understand the impact of these treatments, decides to model the brainwave patterns using advanced mathematical techniques.

1. The brainwave pattern can be represented by a complex-valued function \( \psi(t) = e^{i(\omega t + \phi)} \) where \( \omega \) is the angular frequency and \( \phi \) is the phase shift.
